exhibit.title: Solar System Explorer
exhibit.subtitle: An exhibition of eight worlds, hung three ways
exhibit.intro: Walk the corridor from the Sun outwards. Each planet is a specimen on the ecliptic line. Re-hang the collection — a hang is simply the museum word for an arrangement — to compare size, distance, or the length of days and years.
exhibit.errorCopy: Planet data failed to load. Check that data/planets.json was published with the build, then reload.

views.label: Distance
views.shortLabel: Distances compressed on a log ruler
views.caveat: Log ruler: each step right multiplies the distance from the Sun. True scale would put Neptune 30× farther than Earth — no screen can hold that.

views.label: Size
views.caveat: Radii are compressed so Mercury stays visible beside Jupiter — truly 11 Earths span Jupiter's face. The exact numbers ride every plate.

views.label: Day & Year
views.caveat: Day rings spin at normalized speeds — Venus truly turns 243× slower than Earth, which would look frozen. The readouts keep the truth.

compare.title: Compare specimens
compare.intro: Choose up to three planets. Their measurements line up row by row — bars are on a log scale, numbers are exact.
compare.pickNone: Pick planets above to line them up here.

quiz.title: Curator's challenge
quiz.intro: Two ways to test your orbital instincts — order the planets, or match a record to its holder. No timers, no scores to lose.
quiz.sortIntro: Drag the medallions into order from the Sun outwards — or lift with Enter and move with the arrow buttons.
quiz.place: tap to place a planet here
quiz.correct: That is the Solar System, inner to outer. {first} through {last}.
quiz.incorrect: Not yet — {count} of 8 stand in the right place. The brass-edged ones are settled; lift the others and try again.
quiz.allPlacedHint: All eight placed — check your work when ready.
quiz.matchIntro: Which planet holds this record? Choose one medallion.

caveatPanel.title: Reading this atlas
body: This corridor is honest about being a diagram. Real space is mostly emptiness: line up the true sizes and true distances on one screen and every planet becomes a pixel.

So each hang compresses one thing and labels the compromise. Distance uses a logarithmic ruler. Size compresses radii so Mercury stays visible beside Jupiter. Day and year rings spin at normalized speeds with the true ratios printed beside them.
Whenever you see a bar, ring or sphere, the exact number stands next to it in mono type — trust the number, sense the scale.
